items.title: Pro-Life Group Reportedly Kicked Out of Coffee Shop, Compared to KKK
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: The founder of a well-known pro-life organization has gone viral in recent days after reportedly being kicked out of an […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The founder of a well-known pro-life organization has gone viral in recent days after reportedly being kicked out of an Idaho coffee shop after the owner learned she was holding a meeting there.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Kristan Hawkins, president of Students for Life of America, shared a video of what purportedly took place at Wydaho Roasters last month — and that video went viral.

Hawkins told CBN News that coffee shop owner Jim Sheehan made his displeasure known after she, her son, and others met to discuss pro-life issues inside Wydaho Roasters. Her son’s goal has been to rally people against Proposition 1, an abortion measure that will be on the ballot in November.

“We’re recruiting door knockers, and we’ve had students going door to door, educating people in Idaho about this extreme abortion ballot referendum, which sadly many people don’t know about,” Hawkins said, noting her son rallied people online to come meet to form a pro-life group to address the issue.

The coffee shop was the intended gathering place for the group’s first meeting, but that didn’t go very well.

“We had purchased our drinks and our food,” she said. “Some other leaders, community members, came to kind of join the group that I knew from church.”

According to Hawkins, Sheehan came out of his office and told the group they couldn’t meet at the shop and needed to leave. Hawkins took out her camera and started filming the interaction, hoping she could simply convince the owner to let them stay for the first meeting and then pledge not to return.

“I was trying to negotiate with him, just like, let us finish this meeting; we won’t come back,” she said. “And then he just kept going and then compared us to the KKK and said, we were like the KKK, that pro-lifers were like the KKK, which was just beyond the pale. And that’s actually why I decided to release the video.”

Hawkins made it clear that she believes, as an owner, Sheehan has the right to refuse service and was within his rights to ask the group to leave. That said, she also believes in her right to expose his purported comparison between the pro-life activists and the KKK.

The result of the entire escapade was intense media coverage and viral video discussion. Ultimately, both Hawkins and Sheehan reportedly started getting death threats.

“He was well within his rights to kick us out,” Hawkins said. “I was within my rights to expose his insanity, believing that community members were like the KKK, but neither of us deserves to die or receive death threats.”

Sheehan told Fox News that he pushes back on claims the group was kicked out. He said he had asked via Facebook the day before that the group not meet in his coffee shop.

“Sunday she announced on a local community page they were holding this meeting at our business, naming it — I responded to the post politely asking them not to use our business as the agenda of the organization does not align with us,” he told the outlet. “They showed up anyway.”

items.title: Christian Grandma Refuses to Back Down After Government Demands She Stop Feeding Community
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: What started as a woman feeling called to cook breakfast for a handful of friends has turned into a dispute […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

What started as a woman feeling called to cook breakfast for a handful of friends has turned into a dispute over food, faith, and government regulations.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Kathy Kite, a resident of Harrisburg, Missouri, began welcoming locals into her home for breakfast back in May after the community’s convenience store stopped serving breakfast following COVID.

Kite works at H-Town, the local convenience store and gas station, and said residents had repeatedly expressed interest in finding a new place to have breakfast. She lives nearby, so she decided to offer an alternative by cooking for her friends and offering up the food for free.

“I told the old guys that come in there in the mornings that like to play cards, and drink coffee, and eat breakfast, and say they didn’t have any more — I’m like, ‘You guys can come to my house and I’ll do it,’” Kite told CBN News.

So, she started offering breakfast out of her kitchen and people came.

“It all started with just some like sausage, egg, and cheese biscuits,” Kite said.

At first, it was just a few people. But others soon began to come after her loving act was advertised on social media, with 20-25 people regularly coming to her home in the morning; some parents even brought their kids to her house for food before school. Kite gets up at 3:30 a.m. to prepare for the day.

“And it just kind of exploded from there,” Kite said. “So then people were like, ‘Breakfast? We have breakfast in town?’”

Kite doesn’t charge for the meals. There is a place for people to leave money if they choose, but she said those contributions go back into buying ingredients and food.

“It’s not a moneymaker by any means,” she said.

For Kite, feeding people is also deeply connected to her Christian faith.

“For whatever reason, God has put it in my heart that I need to take care of people,” she said. “I like to feed people.”

Kite continued, “In my mind feeding people is loving people.”

But Kite’s breakfast gatherings eventually caught the attention of government officials, with Columbia city officials from the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department reportedly sending a letter telling her she needed a commercial kitchen license to continue operating.

Kite disputes that she is operating a business, though, and said the government’s demands have broken her heart.

“I’m not running a business,” she said. “This is just friends coming over for breakfast. It’s no different than a backyard barbecue or a church gathering.”

Kite said the warning dramatically affected attendance, as some residents became concerned that continuing to visit could cause additional trouble for her. As a result, many stopped coming.

“I went from having probably 20 to 25 to maybe 5 to 8 people,” she said.

Still, Kite isn’t planning to stop, despite admitting she was scared to incur fines or worse. Rather than back down, she sought legal help and has no plans to stop.

“God laid this on me and I just feel like if God brought me to it, God’s going to bring me through it,” Kite said. “I believe in what I’m doing. I don’t believe I’m doing anything wrong.”

The Goldwater Institute is helping Kite and has sent a letter to the Boone County health department seeking answers about why they are demanding a commercial kitchen. Officials with the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department told Fox News that Kite has a tip jar, open sign, and is advertising food on social media, indicating elements “associated with a food establishment.”

“No citations or cease-and-desist orders were issued. We also did not threaten jail time,” the statement read. “We sent a letter to Ms. Kite following a complaint we received that food served in her establishment made someone ill. Our role in public health is to work with food establishments to promote safe food practices and prevent food-borne illnesses.”

The text continued, “There are safe, allowable ways to provide homemade food to the community with and without a food permit. We regularly work together with individuals and businesses who want to provide free food to the community.”

items.title: The Celebrity Pastor Era Finally Ended. But Then Christian Influencers Took Its Spot.
items.author: Annie Eisner
items.summary: The American church has always had a thing for celebrity — but something shifted over the past five years. We used to point to cool megachurch pastors befriending high-profile believers as proof that Christianity still had cultural pull. Then came a stretch of very public pastoral scandals — resigna
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

The American church has always had a thing for celebrity — but something shifted over the past five years.

We used to point to cool megachurch pastors befriending high-profile believers as proof that Christianity still had cultural pull. Then came a stretch of very public pastoral scandals — resignations, affairs, whole ministries unraveling in real time — and the shine wore off fast.

The allure of charismatic pastors in designer clothes started to feel less like access and more like a mirage. For a generation already skeptical of institutions, the curtain had been pulled back on the Celebrity Pastor Industrial Complex.

Beaty is careful not to vilify the instinct. “Celebrities need Jesus too, so I’m sure there are very good things about these friendships,” she said of celebrity believers. “We attach to them, in part because it lends credibility to a faith that seems weird to a lot of our neighbors. We want to feel like, ‘See? We’re not that weird.’ It lends cultural credibility to our faith.”

But while one kind of platform crumbled, another rose. In place of celebrity pastors, today we have the Christian influencer.

These are people who might not lead a church or hold theological degrees, but they rack up millions of views by talking about God online. Whether it’s an aesthetic devotional or a car confessional, they’re massively popular.

“There’s been a significant decline in trust in institutions,” said author Katelyn Beaty, whose book Celebrities for Jesus explores how platform culture has changed the American church. “In their place, I think many Americans are predisposed to attach themselves to individual figures, most of whom they’ve never encountered in any personal way. But these individuals come to not only symbolize some kind of value or aspiration or political ideology, but also a theological flavor.”

Social media makes these relationships feel personal — like the audience actually knows these people, can trust them, can build a spiritual framework around their content.

But influence doesn’t always mean formation, and visibility doesn’t guarantee wisdom. Many of these creators are new to faith themselves — sincere, maybe even inspiring, but not elders, not pastors, and not accountable to anyone.

“Because of the spiritual emphases of the evangelical movement, there tends to be a distrust of institutions,” Beaty said. “You have to have this born again, highly individualistic experience of salvation, and that often comes through the preaching of a specific evangelist or writer. So I think it is something in the water in American evangelicalism, that we are suspicious of institutions because we don’t really believe they do dynamic work for the Kingdom.”

That suspicion now extends to the church itself — especially among younger Christians who’ve watched spiritual abuse, manipulation or hypocrisy play out up close, and come away disillusioned. Instead of plugging into a church, they log into Instagram or YouTube for spiritual nourishment from someone who feels more relatable, less institutional — more real.

“I wonder if we are actually in a time when the church is going to have to accept becoming smaller and more obscure,” Beaty said. “It’s not going to feel successful. It’s going to feel scary and like maybe God isn’t blessing us.”

But that kind of refinement doesn’t trend. What trends is someone with camera presence, a compelling personal story and the ability to make faith content feel fresh and algorithmically appealing. The line between Christian encouragement and influencer branding blurs — and so does the line between encouragement and authority.

That instinct isn’t inherently bad here either — a video about faith reaching millions of people isn’t a problem on its own. But discipleship doesn’t show up in follower counts or video views.

“So much of the American church has mimicked secular business principles to evaluate success,” Beaty said. “And what we are after, as people attesting to the reality of God in our lives, is not a number of butts in the pews. The metric of discipleship is that you’re actually becoming a community where people are being formed into the likeness of Christ.”

So who is forming us? Who are we actually being discipled by?

If we’re being honest, many of us spend more time listening to Christian influencers than we do talking about our faith in community. We’re not building church families — we’re building an algorithm.

The problem isn’t that influencers talk about Jesus. It’s that we don’t ask who they’re accountable to. We ask how many followers they have. There’s no social media metric for spiritual maturity, and no viral moment that substitutes for long-haul discipleship. There’s no shortcut to Christlikeness — only community, humility and time.

“What if the smaller church and the more localized understanding of Christian discipleship is a way that we are being refined,” Beaty said, “so that the Gospel we attest to actually has staying power and real credibility among our neighbors?”

That’s not glamorous. But it might be the kind of credibility the world actually needs.

items.title: James Joyce, a Priest of the Eternal Imagination
items.author: Matthew Malone
items.summary:
Matthew Malone

The Catholic intellectual and imaginative tradition remained intrinsic to the grammar of his artistic vision.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Matthew Malone

James Joyce is widely regarded as one of the greatest and most enigmatic writers of the twentieth century. Through groundbreaking works, such as Ulysses (1922) and Finnegans Wake (1939), Joyce irreversibly transformed literature by pioneering techniques using stream of consciousness, linguistic experimentation, and complex narrative structures. He arguably created some of the most elegant and beautiful prose in human history, and his innovations revolutionized fiction, reshaping the English language for the modern era. Yet for all Joyce’s profoundly modernist literary contributions, his contemporary, T. S. Eliot, described his work as “penetrated with Christian feeling” with his close friend, Mary Colum, observing, “I have never known anyone with a mind so fundamentally Catholic in structure as Joyce’s own, or one on whom the Church, its ceremonies, symbols, and theological declarations had made such an impression.” Here is a sketch of James Joyce’s biography and his paradoxical relationship with Catholicism. 

James Augustine Aloysius Joyce was born on February 2, 1882, to John Stanislaus and Mary Jane Joyce. James was baptized three days later in St Joseph’s Church in Terenure, a suburb of Dublin. He began his education in 1888 and attended the Jesuit-run Belvedere College in Dublin. As a nine-year-old, James composed his first independently printed work, a short poem called “Et Tu Healy” about the death of Irish nationalist, Charles Stewart Parnell. In 1895, he was elected as a member of the Marian society, Sodality of Our Lady, and was taught a Jesuit education. The young Joyce was educated in Catholic theology, classical philosophy (particularly the work of Aristotle), Latin, and Greek, winning an award for English in his final years at the college. 

In 1898, he enrolled at University College to study languages. He became immersed in the work of St. Thomas Aquinas, who would be formative and significant to Joyce for the rest of his life. In a poem “The Holy Office” (1905) Joyce wrote, “Those souls that hate the strength that mine has, steeled in the school of old Aquinas,” and in a lecture titled “Ireland: Island of Saints and Sages”(1907), Joyce expressed uncharacteristically high acclaim for Aquinas, stating “Two or three illustrious names shine here like the last few stars of radiant night that wanes as dawn arrives. . . . St. Thomas Aquinas, perhaps the keenest and most lucid mind known to human history.” 

In his University College years, Joyce had begun to sincerely question and reject his Catholic faith. His repudiation culminated with the death of his devout mother in August 1903 when she was forty-four. She implored the rebellious James to kneel and pray beside her sick bed, to which the young Joyce refused, marking a pivotal psychological and spiritual moment. Joyce carried the guilt for the remainder of his life, with the scene cropping up repeatedly in his fiction and letters. In June of the following year, Joyce met Nora Barnacle. She became his muse, companion, and lifelong partner. He wrote to her with an obsessive passion throughout his life. In an early letter, Joyce reflected on his break from Catholicism and the Church: 

Six years ago I left the Catholic Church, hating it most fervently. I found it impossible for me to remain in it on account of the impulses of my nature. I made a secret war upon it when I was a student and declined to accept the positions it offered me. By doing this I made myself a beggar but I retained my pride.

Yet as he declared his rejection of Catholicism, he instinctively reached for Biblical language, imagery, and symbolism when expressing his deepest emotions. Writing to Nora six years later, he described his love in an unmistakably Christian vocabulary: 

I too have felt at moments the burning in my soul of that pure and sacred fire which burns forever on the altar of my love’s heart. I could have knelt by that little bed and abandoned myself to a flood of tears. . . . I could have knelt and prayed there as the three kings from the East knelt and prayed before the manger in which Jesus lay. They had travelled over deserts and seas and brought gifts and wisdom and royal trains to kneel before a little new-born child and I had brought my errors and follies and sins and wondering and longing to lay them at the little bed in which a young girl had dreamed of me.

This tension between renunciation and inheritance characterized a major thread for Joyce in his life and work. Joyce may have rejected Catholicism, but Catholicism had not rejected him. The Catholic intellectual and imaginative tradition remained intrinsic to the grammar of his artistic vision. 

Joyce’s first major work, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916), follows the spiritual and intellectual development of his fictional alter ego, Stephen Dedalus. The novel traces Stephen’s journey from childhood to early adulthood as he confronts faith and doubt, passing through phases of intense religious devotion and reckless hedonism. A key component of the novel is Stephen’s struggle between Catholic priesthood and an artistic vocation. Stephen defines the artist as “the priest of the eternal imagination transmuting the daily bread of experience into the radiant body of everliving life.” The language is undeniably sacramental just as the priest transforms ordinary bread into the Body of Christ through Eucharistic consecration, the artist transforms the ordinary material of human life into art. In A Portrait, Stephen also adapts Aquinas’s three conditions of beauty—integritas, consonantia, and claritas— into his own aesthetic theory as the fundamental principles through which the artist understands, orders, and reveals the eternal nature of reality.

The struggle between priest and artist culminates in a scene where the Jesuit Director of Belvedere asks Stephen to consider a priestly vocation:

A flame began to flutter again on Stephen’s cheek as he heard in this proud address an echo of his own proud musings. How often had he seen himself as a priest wielding calmly and humbly the awful power of which angels and saints stood in reverence! His soul had loved to muse in secret on this desire. He had seen himself, a young and silent-mannered priest, entering a confessional swiftly, ascending the altarsteps, incensing, genuflecting, accomplishing the vague acts of the priesthood which pleased him by reason of their semblance of reality and of their distance from it. In that dim life which he had lived through in his musings he had assumed the voices and gestures which he had noted with various priests. He had bent his knee sideways like such a one, he had shaken the thurible only slightly like such a one, his chasuble had swung open like that of such another as he turned to the altar again after having blessed the people. . . . No touch of sin would linger upon the hands with which he would elevate and break the host; no touch of sin would linger on his lips in prayer to make him eat and drink damnation to himself not discerning the body of the Lord. He would hold his secret knowledge and secret power, being as sinless as the innocent: and he would be a priest forever according to the order of Melchisedec.

Joyce rejected the Catholic priesthood, but retained its deepest structure, recasting the artist as the witness and mediator between God and the fallen world. The host, chalice, and altar give way to the pen, page, and book as the path to reveal the divine in the ordinary. Throughout A Portrait, there are countless examples of Catholic contemplation and ambiguous feelings toward the Church. One moving example is the passage when Stephen goes to confession. Few authors have captured the feeling with such psychological honesty and elation as Joyce: 

He knelt to say his penance, praying in a corner of the dark nave: and his prayers ascended to heaven from his purified heart like perfume streaming upwards from a heart of white rose. The muddy streets were gay. He strode homeward, conscious of an invisible grace pervading and making light his limbs. In spite of all he had done it. He had confessed and God had pardoned him. His soul was made fair and holy once more, holy and happy. It would be beautiful to die if God so willed. It was beautiful to live in grace a life of peace and virtue and forbearance with others. He sat by the fire in the kitchen, not daring to speak for happiness. Till that moment he had not known how beautiful and peaceful life could be. The green square of paper pinned round the lamp cast down a tender shade. On the dresser was a plate of sausages and white pudding and on the shelf there were eggs. They would be for the breakfast in the morning after the communion in the college chapel. White pudding and eggs and sausages and cups of tea. How simple and beautiful was life after all! And life lay all before him.

For Dedalus, the sacrament of confession is a moving encounter with grace. Joyce illustrates the experience with astonishing sincerity, painting the moment when grace transfigures the world, elevating the most mundane details—from the “muddy streets” of Dublin to a breakfast of “sausages and white pudding”—with levity, beauty, and hope. It also reminds us that sacramental action has the power to inspire faith amid doubt. The scene also suggests that while the feeling may be momentary, grace leaves a permanent impression upon the human heart. The faith, formation, and sacramental imagination that Joyce experienced left an unalterable imprint upon his mind and soul that continued to inform, shape, and frame his artistic and intellectual vision long after he had verbally rejected the Church. Perhaps this is revealed most convincingly in his follow-up work, Ulysses, described by Joyce’s friend Mary Colum as “one of the most Catholic books ever written.” 

Ulysses tells the story of Leopold Bloom through a single day in Dublin, June 16, 1904, whilst Joyce’s alter-ego Stephen Dedalus wanders the city. The book is shaped by Homer’s The Odyssey with Bloom functioning as an everyday Odysseus who goes about his day of eating, drinking, arguing, and encountering strangers confronting themes of mortality, sexuality, religion, exile, and the fundamental search for meaning. Ulysses is littered with Catholic references and concerns. Early in the novel, Joyce recounts through Dedalus his refusal to kneel and pray at his mother’s bedside, establishing from the outset the theme of guilt and conflict with Catholicism: 

A cloud began to cover the sun slowly, shadowing the bay in deeper green. It lay behind him, a bowl of bitter waters. . . . Silent with awe and pity I went to her bedside. She was crying in her wretched bed. For those words, Stephen: love’s bitter mystery. . . . Memories beset his brooding brain. Her glass of water from the kitchen tap when she had approached the sacrament. . . . Her eyes on me to strike me down. Liliata rutilantium te confessorum turma circumdet: iubilantium te virginum chorus excipiat / May the lilied throng of radiant confessors surround you: may the choir of jubilant virgins welcome you. . . . No mother. Let me be and let me live.” 

One of the most memorable Catholic episodes in the novel is when Joyce takes us into Bloom’s stream of consciousness as he stumbles into Mass. Unlike Dedalus, who has internalized the Church’s theology, Bloom is a Jewish outsider observing Catholic ritual with wonder and skepticism: 

He approached a bench and seated himself in its corner, nursing his hat and newspaper. . . . Yes, bread of angels it’s called. There’s a big idea behind it, kind of kingdom of God is within you feel. . . . Thing is if you really believe in it. Lourdes cure, waters of oblivion, and the Knock apparition, statues bleeding. Old fellow asleep near the confession box . . . Blind faith. Safe in the arms of the kingdom come. . . . He saw the priest stow the communion cup away . . . letters on his back I.N.R.I.? No: I.H.S. Molly told me one time I asked her. I have sinned: or no: I have suffered, it is. And the other one? Iron nails ran in. 

The two central characters, Catholic-formed Dedalus and middle-class Jew Bloom, converge in a penultimate episode, engaging in a question and answer style conversation, described by Joyce as written in “catechism (impersonal)” technique and as the “mathematico-astronomico-physico-mechanico-geometrico-chemico sublimation of Bloom and Stephen.” The dialogue unites the characters in an interplay between the mundane and the transcendent as they discuss the microcosm of the day and the macrocosm of the cosmos. 
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

Throughout Ulysses, Joyce repeatedly substitutes traditional religious experience with ordinary human life, illuminating the spiritual dimensions within it. In this way, Joyce recalls Caravaggio, who brought contemporary life into his paintings, using ordinary Romans, street people, and prostitutes as models for saints. For Caravaggio as for Joyce, the sacred is not in some remote idealized world; it is within the gritty imperfections of human life. 

In many respects, this echoes the Gospel scenes of Christ walking and talking amongst the ordinary people amidst the mundanity of daily life, sanctifying their reality by his presence. Jesus eats with sinners, touches the unclean, speaks with the marginalized, and takes unleavened bread and offers it as his body. The Incarnation itself is the ultimate elevation of the ordinary—God entering human history, assuming our flesh, and living amongst us. Through an encounter with Christ, the world is transfigured and imbued with profound meaning, beauty, and luminosity, reminding us that creation can become a medium through which the divine is encountered. This is the artistic principle Joyce inherits and transforms, the artist finds within the seemingly mundane world the possibility of revelation. 

James Joyce died on January 13, 1941, at the age of fifty-eight. There were rumors abounding as to whether Joyce had gone back to his Catholicism upon his deathbed, with Joseph Walshe, secretary at the Department of External Affairs in Dublin, writing, “Please wire details of Joyce’s death. If possible find out, did he die a Catholic?” Nora Barnacle declined the offer for a Catholic burial and even though Joyce renounced the Church, it is reported that he occasionally went to Mass on Holy Thursday and Good Friday throughout his life. Joyce remained an enigma until the end. 

James Joyce was a deeply complex and paradoxical talent who appeared to reject Catholicism yet retained its sacramental imagination, transposing it into a secular literary context. He adapted the Catholic conviction of the Incarnation and revealed it in the whole of human experience. He resented the institution of the Church, yet the institutional formation he received from the Jesuits gave Joyce the intellectual freedom and framework through which he would create. This is the crux of the Joyce paradox: The Catholicism he rejected furnished the very imagination through which he would continue to explore the eternal. Whether conscious or not, Joyce bears a remarkable resemblance to the Catholic vision he inherited—the extraordinary discovered within the ordinary, the sacred within the profane, beauty within the mundane, and the transcendent glimpsed through the mortal. He rejected the priesthood, but the sacramental imagination remained. The altar gave way to the page, the liturgy to literature, and the priestly act of mediation to the artist’s attempt to reveal the eternal within the everyday.

items.title: Friday, September 4, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, people ask Jesus why he doesn’t encourage fasting among his followers.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
1 Corinthians 4:1-5

Think of us in this way, as servants of Christ and stewards of God’s mysteries. Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found trustworthy. But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. I do not even judge myself. I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me. Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive commendation from God.

Psalm
Psalm 37:3-4, 5-6, 27-28, 39-40

Trust in the Lord, and do good;
    so you will live in the land, and enjoy security.
Take delight in the Lord,
    and he will give you the desires of your heart.
Commit your way to the Lord;
    trust in him, and he will act.
He will make your vindication shine like the light,
    and the justice of your cause like the noonday.
Depart from evil, and do good;
    so you shall abide forever.
For the Lord loves justice;
    he will not forsake his faithful ones.
The righteous shall be kept safe forever,
    but the children of the wicked shall be cut off.
The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord;
    he is their refuge in the time of trouble.
The Lord helps them and rescues them;
    he rescues them from the wicked, and saves them,
    because they take refuge in him.

Gospel Reading
Luke 5:33-39

Then they said to him, “John’s disciples, like the disciples of the Pharisees, frequently fast and pray, but your disciples eat and drink.” Jesus said to them, “You cannot make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them, can you? The days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece from a new garment and sews it on an old garment; otherwise the new will be torn, and the piece from the new will not match the old. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the new wine will burst the skins and will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins. And no one after drinking old wine desires new wine, but says, ‘The old is good.’”

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, people ask Jesus why he doesn’t encourage fasting among his followers. Jesus’s answer is wonderful: “Can you make the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (That’s a typically Jewish style, by the way, answering a question with another question.)

This great image of the wedding feast comes up frequently in the New Testament, most obviously in the wedding feast at Cana narrative. And it is echoed in the tradition. Jesus is the wedding of heaven and earth, the marriage of divinity and humanity; he is the bridegroom and the Church is the bride. In him, the most intimate union is achieved between God and the world.

Could you imagine people fasting at a wedding banquet? Could you imagine going into an elegant room with your fellow guests and being served bread and water? It would be ridiculous! The mark of the Christian dispensation is joy. Exuberance. Delight. God and the world have come together. What could be better news?
